provenance.note: Juniperus virginiana (eastern redcedar) is the drawable stand-in for Juniperus occidentalis (Oregon juniper), the low, wide, wind-hardy juniper that forms the native juniper woodland of the Harney Basin and the windbreak on a high-desert ranch lot. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn; the drawable taxon is an eastern species, so the rendered crown is narrower and taller than a real Oregon juniper. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on J. occidentalis. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 3.0 among the lot's trees, the largest share, because on this lot the juniper is the shelter that everything else depends on; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: The drawable taxon Pinus ponderosa stands in for itself: ponderosa pine is the pine of the Blue Mountains immediately north of Burns, where the Hines lumber company cut it from 1928, and it is a planted conifer on ranch shelterbelts further out on the plateau. It is used here as its own stand-in, which is the honest choice because the species is both native to the region and present in the drawable list. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the model's own, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 0.6 among the lot's trees, kept low because at 35 m and a 12.9 m crown this is the one entry wide and tall enough to fill a small rural plot on its own; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: The drawable taxon Calocedrus decurrens stands in for itself: incense-cedar is native to south-central and southwestern Oregon's mountain slopes, within the same ecoregion as the Blue Mountains north of Burns, and appears as a planted windbreak and shelterbelt in the high desert. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the model's own, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 0.4 among the lot's trees, the lowest of the three conifers, because at 40 m tall and 13.5 m across it is a very large plant for a small rural plot and the importer will place it last; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: Crataegus crus-galli (cockspur hawthorn) is the drawable stand-in for Crataegus douglasii (black hawthorn), the hawthorn of Oregon's sagebrush slopes and canyon country, planted as a hedgerow tree and small windbreak on ranch lots, and the only Crataegus in the drawable list. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on C. douglasii. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 2.0 among the lot's trees, second largest, because a thorny small hawthorn is the plant that gives the sage thrasher and the black-billed magpie somewhere to nest; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: Amelanchier arborea (downy serviceberry) is the drawable stand-in for Amelanchier alnifolia (Saskatoon serviceberry), a native shrubby tree of dry slopes and draws throughout eastern Oregon that is widely planted around farmsteads for its fruit and its erosion-rooting habit. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn; the two species are congeners with a similar habit, so the substitution is close rather than forced. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on A. alnifolia. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 2.5 among the lot's trees, because a berry-bearing native that fruits in the cold season is one of the few food sources the lot's winter birds have; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: The drawable taxon Acer negundo stands in for itself: boxelder is native to Oregon and is the common pioneer maple of the dry creek draws and irrigated ditches around a Harney Basin ranch, tolerant of the alkaline, seasonally flooded ground where the Columbia spotted frog breeds. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the model's own, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 2.0 among the lot's trees, because it is the one deciduous that follows water, which is what ties the planted part of this lot to the wet ground the frog needs; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: Fraxinus pennsylvanica (green ash) is the drawable stand-in for Fraxinus latifolia (Oregon ash), the riparian ash of Oregon's wet draws; the drawable F. pennsylvanica is an eastern species, so it is a substitute rather than a match, but it is the only Fraxinus in the drawable list and the two are closely related. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on F. latifolia. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 1.5 among the lot's trees, below the boxelder because a ranch lot has less wet ground than a creek draw; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

speeeecies contributors, schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json (drawable plant models), CC BY-SA 4.0

provenance.note: Populus deltoides (eastern cottonwood) is the drawable stand-in for Populus tremuloides (quaking aspen), which forms the aspen stands on the moister northern and higher parts of the Harney Basin and on the Blue Mountain foothills north of Burns. The drawable P. deltoides is an eastern species with a much wider crown than a real aspen, so the rendered plant will look broader than it should; that is a property of the drawn model, which is why the validator's size rule is satisfied by copying the model's own numbers rather than aspen's real ones. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on P. tremuloides. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 0.3, the lowest in this catalog, because at a 30.7 m crown this is the one entry certain to be dropped or badly spaced in a small rural plot, and docs/locale-richness.md advises keeping wide-crowned trees to one or two at low weight; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.

provenance.note: Salix nigra (black willow) is the drawable stand-in for Salix exigua (sandbar willow), the narrow-leaf willow that lines the Harney Basin's ditches, creek margins and pond edges and is the dominant woody plant in the wet ground this lot's frog depends on. The drawable S. nigra is a larger eastern river willow, so the rendered plant is a coarse substitute for what is really a slender basin willow; it is the only Salix in the drawable list. Growth form, evergreen flag, height_m and crown_width_m are the stand-in model's, from schema/v0.1/flora-taxa.json, so placement matches what is drawn. native_status follows the Wikipedia article on S. exigua. community_weight is judgement: a relative share of 1.5 among the lot's trees, because willow is what makes the pond edge read as Harney Basin rather than as a garden pond; divided by the importer's 1.0 multiplier for Native plants.
